docs.title: VHS-Decode - Part 1
docs.text:
This tutorial is exclusively for capturing VHS tapes

This tutorial (or rather blog) shows you start to end on how to do your very first video-only capture with vhs-decode in Linux. Capturing audio and improving the quality will come in later parts of this blog (if I manage to understand it :laught:). It's meant for absolute beginners, although it's assumed that you have some basic technical understanding + skills and know how to use the terminal in Linux.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
• Basic soldering skills
  • Basic Linux & Terminal understanding (includes knowing common commands, e.g. changing directory, moving files, ...)

docs.title: Main parts
docs.text:
• PC with two spare PCIe slots and Linux as OS: For beginners preferred Linux Mint or at least Debian based (Linux Mint is based on Ubuntu which is based on Debian), most other distros work too, but in that case you should really know your distro.
  • VCR (Video Cassette Recorder) (your VHS player)
  • Optional: TV/Monitor for the VCR (just for viewing the tape during capture)

docs.title: Miscellaneous parts for vhs-decode
docs.text:
• Soldering iron and belonging tools

  • CX Card(s) (you'll need two of them to capture video and audio because VHS uses two channels, but in this first test we're only going to capture video, so one is enough for now)

  • BNC Female Jack Bulkhead To SMA Male SMA Plug

  • SMA Male to SMA Male (or two separate male cables with no connector at the other end, but I found it's easier to find a male to male cable and just cut it in half)

  • RG316 BNC Male to BNC Male

  • BNC Female Right Angle 90 Degree Plug (make sure they look like in this image, there are lots of different variants and this is the one that fits to the CX cards)

  • 10uF Capacitor, preferred ceramic but if you have a spare electrolytic it'll do, but there you need to be aware of the polarization (or just directly go with the amplifier from the ko-fi store, but as of writing this, I haven't fully understood it myself and are just in the first capture stage)

  • Optional: 40x40mm heatsinks - for the CX Cards to prevent overheating

To make it clear if you're a bit overwhelmed with all the connectors: These are really only for convenience. Theoretically, just a long enough bare coaxial cable would be enough, the connectors are just for convenience to allow you unplugging it and integrating the amplifier (you don't need to know about the amplifier yet).

For all the cables you should get ones with 50 Ohm (usually specified in the product title or description).

For the length, you should just measure how much you need and order ones as short as possible to avoid interference. But don't use too short ones to avoid wiring problems later on.

docs.title: Start
docs.text:
Okay, so let's start. If you're reading this and haven't ordered your parts yet or you currently wait for them to arrive, keep on reading to get a better understanding of how it works. It'll help reading this (and the official vhs-decode wiki) multiple times, with some time between. You can also do some preparation already.

First, find a place to put your VCR and (preferred dedicated) capture PC.

Take a note of your VCR model name. Remove the cover from your VCR (most of the time the screws are on the sides and back).

docs.title: Finding the test point
docs.text:
For finding the test points, you should follow the official WIKI. As said, in the first step we're only going to capture video so we just need to find the video test point, although it won't hurt searching for the audio test point too. Note that if your VCR does not have Hi-Fi audio support (most of the time it's written on the tape cover on the front of your VCR), you won't find a audio test point because this test point is ONLY for capturing the Hi-Fi (better quality) audio. Not all VCRs support that and not all tapes have Hi-Fi audio in the first place. That means if your tape doesn't have Hi-Fi audio the Hi-Fi test point will be completely useless even if your VCR has one. In that case you'll need to capture the standard way with the standard audio output at the back of the VCR.

VHS-Decode links for finding test points:

  • General info: RF Tapping · oyvindln/vhs-decode Wiki · GitHub
  • List of already found test points (check if your model is in there): 004 The Tap List · oyvindln/vhs-decode Wiki · GitHub
  • Reports (check if your model (or manufacturer) is in there to get more info about your model): VCR reports · oyvindln/vhs-decode Wiki · GitHub

If you can't find the test points by looking at the PCBs inside of the VCR, search the web for a service manual for your specific model. It's not that easy to read them if you haven't read service manuals before, but it can definitively help. For example in my case there was a white connector with 6 pins on the board, but only labelled with a cryptic name. I found it in the service manuals and there was also the description what each pin does, one of them was the test point that we need. If your service manual contains a troubleshooting section, that can be very helpful too.

Sadly, it's not always easy to find the correct service manual. If you have luck, you directly find it when searching google for your model number and writing service manual behind it. You'll have issues finding it most of the time if you have a re-branded model (no main brand like JVC, Sony, ...). In my case I have an AGFAPHOTO DV 18909R and I couldn't find a service manual at all. After opening it up and removing the whole tape unit, I saw another model number printed on the mainboard. This revealed the actual manufacturer (which was Daewoo). That still wasn't enough because that model number from the mainboard didn't really exist, but luckily when typing it in google gave me a normal user manual with a VCR that looked identical to mine. And it contained the actual model number of the unit itself. All I had to do was type in this newly found model number and - I got my service manual! All I want to say with this is, it's very likely that your service manual is somewhere out there, you just need to hunt it down.

If you still can't find the test point with the service manual, someone at the vhs-decode subreddit or on the Discord server may be able to help you. But if ask there, you should have your service manual ready to get the best help.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
You've found your test point. If you didn't find it yet, you can skip to CX Cards

Get the SMA male cable with no connector on the other end. Solder that end to the capacitor. Use the official WIKI to find out how to connect the other end of the capacitor to your test point. Now you have a SMA male connector that goes to your test point. Then use the other cables to extend it and to get a final BNC male output. You can also prepare the other cable for Hi-Fi audio capture.

docs.title: CX Cards
docs.text:
First find out what model you've got and if it's good: Types Of CX2388x Cards · happycube/cxadc-linux3 Wiki. The exact model is written on the big chip on the card. They even ship different models if you order multiple at once. For me, one had the CX23883 and the other the CX25800 chip. The CX25800 is the slightly better one, but CX23883 seems to be fine too. For the first video-only capture, I chose to use the CX23883 card as it had the hole for the additional connector already drilled.

Now we're going to do the following mods:

  • RCA to BNC replacement / adding
  • C31 Removal / moving

Optional mods that can be done later: - Cooling Mod

In my case I'm using the 3rd connector (and not replacing the middle connector) because one of the cards already had the hole. For the other one, I'm going to drill the hole myself. After having the BNC connector installed, do the C31 removal (or move it to the other pad if you're using the 3rd connector like I do).

Note: I'm actually unsure if the C31 removal (and BNC Jack mod) should be done for the newer CX25800 cards because in the Types Of CX2388x Cards wiki, recommended mods are only listed for the older CX23883. I don't know if they just forgot to add the recommended mods to the description of the newer card or if it's intentional. However, in the CX Cards wiki, there is no differentiation between card types.

Because I will do the clockgen mod later anyway (which I really recommend to avoid sync issues) and just want to see if it's working at all right now, I'm not going to do the crystal replacement mod.

After your card is ready, install it to your capturing PC.

docs.title: Checking if the card is recognized
docs.text: After installing the driver, the card should be there as /dev/cxadc0. You can check this with this command: ls /dev/cxadc0 If it returns the path, your card is properly recognized! If it says the path cannot be found, something went wrong.

docs.title: Installing the driver
docs.text:
For installing the driver, follow the instructions of the driver's README: GitHub - happycube/cxadc-linux3

First you must install the dependencies, download the repo to your local disk and then build it. After that, reboot and check if the card is recognized.

For installing the dependencies, If you're using a different repo than what's listed there (currently only Ubuntu 22.04 or RPi OS), AI can help relatively good with getting the dependencies that you need to install on your distro. In my case I've use openSUSE. Although it worked for me, I recommend just using a distro (currently Ubuntu) that's supported by the official WIKI if you use a dedicated PC.

docs.title: Connecting the cables
docs.text: Now after the driver is working, it's a good time to connect the cable with the BNC plug from your VCR to the CX card.

docs.title: Find the correct vmux input
docs.text:
The CX cards have 3 inputs, depending on your card and which of the two RCA inputs you've used, you need to find the correct output.

For finding the correct vmuc input, check this wiki: Types Of CX2388x Cards · happycube/cxadc-linux3 Wiki

To configure the correct vmux input, you must execute this command: echo 1 >/sys/class/cxadc/cxadc0/device/parameters/vmux Replace the number after echo with the input you want to use. This is explained here as an example: https://github.com/happycube/cxadc-linux3?tab=readme-ov-file#module-parameters

docs.title: Driver setup
docs.text: You should read trough the driver's README to get an overview of all the things you that you can adjust. I'm not fully sure (because I played around with it because I had no signal at all at first (but at the end the issue was something else, see troubleshooting below)), but I think it's not needed and is only fine adjusting.

docs.title: Testing the signal
docs.text: After successfully installing the driver, we can now finally test if we receive a signal from our VCR. For this, we use ffplay: https://github.com/happycube/cxadc-linux3?tab=readme-ov-file#commands-to-check-for-signal-burst

docs.title: Folder structure
docs.text:
For initial testing, a relatively small disk is okay. But for doing longer captures, you'll need a lot of storage space. For testing, I just made a folder in my home directory. My folder structure as example:

workdir
  captures
    some-capture.u8
  decoded
    some-capture.tbc
    some-capture_chroma.tbc
    some-capture.json
    some-capture.log
  export
    some-capture.mkv
  tools

docs.title: Getting required software
docs.text:
Download the tbc-tools archive and the vhs-decode AppImage from: Releases · oyvindln/vhs-decode · GitHub. Extract the tbc-tools archive into your tools folder. Also place your AppImage there.

Download the tbc-video-export AppImage from: Releases · JuniorIsAJitterbug/tbc-video-export · GitHub

Example:

.
└── workdir/
    └── tools/
        ├── tbc-tools/
        │   ├── 40msps-to-10msps-8-bit-HiFi.sh
        │   ├── ld-compress
        │   ├── tbc-tools-x86_64.AppImage
        │   └── ...
        ├── vhs-decode-x86_64.AppImage
        └── tbc-video-export-v0.1.8-amd64.AppImage

docs.title: Capturing
docs.text:
To capture a 10 seconds clip, execute this command (execute inside of your captures folder): timeout 10s cat /dev/cxadc0 |pv > captures/CX_Card_28msps_8-bit.u8

With that, you receive your capture in this file: CX_Card_28msps_8-bit.u8

docs.title: Decoding
docs.text:
After getting the .u8 file, we can now decode it. In my case the command is: tools/vhs-decode-x86_64.AppImage vhs --debug --tape_format vhs --system pal --cxadc --threads 8 --recheck_phase captures/CX_Card_28msps_8-bit.u8 decoded/CX_Card_28msps_8-bit

For more information, see here: RF Capture Decoding Guide · oyvindln/vhs-decode Wiki · GitHub

Note that the output path does not have a file ending. That's because it will actually create multiple output files.

docs.title: Analysing
docs.text:
Now that we have our .tbc files, we can analyse them by starting ld-analyse (this opens a GUI, it will throw an error if you're doing it over SSH): tools/tbc-tools/tbc-tools-x86_64.AppImage decoded/CX_Card_28msps_8-bit.tbc

Hint: If it's only black & white, press the Source button in the bottom right menu bar to switch to chroma mode

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
Run the export command: tools/tbc-video-export.AppImage --tbc-tools-appimage tools/tbc-tools/tbc-tools-x86_64.AppImage decoded/tape-2025-12-06.01.tbc

Move the exported file to the export folder:mv decoded/*.mkv export

docs.title: Finished!
docs.text:
You can now watch your .mkv file! But as explained at the beginning, we don't have any audio yet and the quality can probably be improved by tuning hardware & software.

Although it isn't needed yet in the testing stage, I still want to mention that you can use tools like Handbrake to encode your .mkv file to make it smaller (depending on the settings you'll lose quality the more you compress it at the reward of disk space).

docs.title: Very bad results
docs.text: When I tried to preview the signal with ffplay and did my first capture, the results were very bad (unusable). But I've just made the very dumb mistake that I did not ground it properly. I just soldered the cable to the video test point but did not solder to the shielding. I'm actually surprised that it worked at all and that it not went up in smokes. To ground it properly, just solder the cable's shielding to some metal inside the VCR. In my case I've used the metal box of the TV signal in/output, you can see the yellow cable in my wiring images above.

docs.title: No signal at all / ffplay shows no noise
docs.text:
Note: If you've got a good connection and no tape is playing, it's normal that there is no noise.

I've had a really weird issue that after powering on / rebooting the PC, there is just no signal at all. No noise. Nothing. Accidentally I found how to make it work: I need to put the PC to sleep (suspend) and then wake it up again. After that, the card works.

Another cause can be a missing or not fully installed driver, especially after OS updates. Follow all the driver install steps again, including the permissions.

docs.title: Extract archives within subfolders (WinRAR)
docs.text:
Having a lot of archived, all in their own sub-folder?

.
└── main-folder/
    ├── sub-folder1/
    │   └── archive.rar
    ├── sub-folder2/
    │   └── archive.rar
    ├── sub-folder3/
    │   └── archive.rar
    └── sub-folder4/
        └── archive.rar

You can extract all of them with this command from the main-folder: 

dir -Recurse | % {$_.FullName} | Split-Path | Get-Unique | % {cd $_ ; & "C:\Program Files\WinRAR\Rar.exe" x *.rar}

I sadly can't currently say if this also works with splitted archives because it's been a while since I used this command and I no longer have a Windows PC nor subfolders with archives in them. But as far as I remember I used it for splitted archives.

docs.title: Sideload an Android App and spoofing the installer
Sideload an Android App and spoofing the installer
docs.text:
When installing an Android app, the system keeps track of where it came from. For example, if you install an app from the Google Play Store, the app info will show something like "Installed from Google Play Store". Normally, it doesn't matter where the app came from, but in some cases like Android Auto, it does.

Android Auto does not show apps that were installed from sources other than Google Play. This prevents you from using modded apps in AA (e.g. Spotify,...).

You can enable developer mode in AA, but in my case, the apps from different sources do not always show up and I have to reconnect AA in hopes it will be there on the next try. With spoofing the installed app, it is way more consistent (however it's still missing sometimes) and you don't need to enable the developer mode.

To do this, you just need to use the -i argument and define the package name of the installer app: 

adb install -i "com.android.vending" -r .\path\to\your.apk

docs.title: Set up Raspberry Pi as web kiosk
Set up Raspberry Pi as web kiosk
Compatibility
docs.text: These instrutions haven't been fully tested from start to end because they were created after I set up the two kiosks I currently have. It should work with any recent Raspberry Pi OS (e.g. 12) though. Let me know if there's a issue somewhere in these instructions.

docs.title: Preparations
docs.text:
• Install the headless RPi OS (if you need to use the desktop variant for some reason, configure it to boot to console)
  • Make sure auto-login is enabled:
    • sudo raspi-config -> 1 System Options -> S6 Auto Login -> Yes
  • Make sure openbox is installed
  • Make sure unclutter is installed (optional, can be commented out in the script below)

docs.title: Display & Browser setup
docs.text:
1. Create/modify the file /home/pi/.xinitrcand add:

    /home/pi/.xinitrc
    #!/bin/bash
openbox-session &
exec /home/pi/kiosk.sh

  2. Set the correct permissions: chmod +x /home/pi/.xinitrc

  3. Create/modify the file /home/pi/.bash_profile and add:

    /home/pi/.bash_profile
    [[ -z $DISPLAY && $XDG_VTNR -eq 1 ]] && startx -- -nocursor

  4. Set the correct permissions: chmod +x /home/pi/.bash_profile

  5. Create the file /home/pi/kiosk.sh and add:

    /home/pi/kiosk.sh
    #!/bin/bash

URL="http://homeassistant.local"
CHROMIUM_PREFERENCES_FILE="/home/$USER/.config/chromium/Default/Preferences"

# Remove mouse cursor (optional)
unclutter -idle 5 -root &

# Disable screensavers (if they are enabled by default)
xset -dpms
xset s off
xset s noblank

# Prevent Chromium addons from automatically updating (which may open a new tab which is then displayed instead of our kiosk page)
sed -i 's|"update_url":"https://clients2.google.com/service/update2/crx"|"update_url":"https://localhost"|' "$CHROMIUM_PREFERENCES_FILE"

# Remove warning popups in Chrome
sed -i 's/"exited_cleanly":false/"exited_cleanly":true/' /home/$USER/.config/chromium/Default/Preferences
sed -i 's/"exit_type":"Crashed"/"exit_type":"Normal"/' /home/$USER/.config/chromium/Default/Preferences

####################################################################################
## Choose your browser by uncommenting either "chromium-browser" or "firefox-esr" ##
####################################################################################

# Launch chromium browser
#chromium-browser --noerrdialogs --disable-infobars --kiosk "$URL"

# Some more chrome flags that can be used:
# --hide-scrollbars

# Launch Firefox
#firefox-esr --kiosk "$URL"

  6. Set the correct permissions: chmod +x /home/pi/kiosk.sh

  7. Reboot. The kiosk should automatically start on the next boot.

docs.title: Custom browser scripts
docs.text:
You can use the browser extension Tampermonkey for writing custom browser scripts. With such a script, you can e.g. automatically fill in form fields and click buttons, very useful if you need to log in somewhere.

In some cases, such a script will not work after rebooting because the browser window may not be focused properly. In that case it can help to (virtually) press a key.

  1. Create a new script, e.g. /home/pi/press-key.sh 

    #!/bin/bash
xdotool key F2

  2. Set the correct permissions: chmod +x /home/pi/press-key.sh

  3. Install a cronjob (crontab -e) 

    # Execute key-press script to focus browser to allow custom scripts
* * * * * DISPLAY=:0 /home/pi/press-key.sh

docs.title: Setup daily reboots
docs.text: To make sure there are no permanent hangs (e.g. a website that no longer refreshes on its own) and to keep the system more reliable, you should set up daily rebooting. You can do this by setting up a cronjob (crontab -e) with: 0 3 * * * sudo reboot

docs.title: Finalize setup
docs.text:
If everything is set up and works correctly, you can enable the overlay file system on the raspberry pi.

  • sudo raspi-config -> 4 Performance Options -> P2 Overlay File System -> Yes -> Ok -> No -> Ok -> Reboot

You can keep the boot partition writeable as normally there isn't written much anyway.

The overlay file system will not only greatly reduce SD card wear but also prevents corruption, full storage issues or similar. This will give you a setup that should require little to no maintenance. For making updates or other changes, don't forget to disable the overlay file system before doing them, otherwise everything will be reverted on the next reboot.

docs.title: What the overlay file system actually does
docs.text: If the overlay file system is enabled, your Raspberry Pi’s root filesystem is mounted as read-only, and a temporary writable layer (in RAM) is placed on top. You can still "write" files (create, edit, or delete them) just like normal, but all changes are stored in the temporary layer. After a reboot, everything is reset to the previous state because the modifications in the temporary layer are discarded and the underlying system remains unchanged. With a standard read-only filesystem, modifying files would not be possible at all.

docs.title: WiFi troubleshooting
docs.text: If you experience conenctivity issues, here are some troubleshooting steps you can try.

docs.title: Find out what's causing issues
docs.text:
Example commands that can help you identify the problem:

  • iw wlan1 link - Check the signal strength (60-70 should be okay, -80 dBm or lower is really bad)
  • sudo journalctl -u wpa_supplicant --since "8 hours ago"
  • sudo journalctl -u NetworkManager --since "8 hours ago"
  • sudo journalctl -b --since "8 hours ago" | grep wlan

docs.title: Set infinity reconnect attempts (untested if that really works)
docs.text:
Create and edit the file /etc/NetworkManager/conf.d/99-retry.conf: 

[connection]
autoconnect-retries=0  # 0 means infinite

docs.title: For hidden networks (currently not sure if it really improves anything, we'll see)
docs.text: Make sure that your network service knows that it's hidden.

docs.title: If using nmcli
docs.text: Type nmcli connection show <network-name> and look for the line 802-11-wireless.hidden. If it's set to yes and your network is hidden, it's already set up correctly. If it's set to no, you should set it to yes with sudo nmcli connection modify <network-name> 802-11-wireless.hidden yes

docs.title: If using wpa_supplicant directly
docs.text: Add this line in your network config, e.g. add it below psk=xxx: scan_ssid=1

docs.title: How to find out what you're using
docs.text: If /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf contains your network config, you're using wpa_supplicant directly. If /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf does not contain your network config or does not exist at all, you're likely not using wpa_supplicant. Check if the command nmcli connection show shows your connected wifi network. If it shows it, you're using nmcli.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi: Network boot with the root filesystem on iSCSI
Raspberry Pi: Network boot with the root filesystem on iSCSI
docs.text:
AI-generated guide

This guide was written by an AI. I did not write the text myself. I did, however, carry out the procedure on a Raspberry Pi 3B with Raspberry Pi OS Lite 64-bit (Trixie), a Debian 13 Netboot VM on Proxmox and OPNsense with Dnsmasq, and the Pi now boots entirely over the network. The steps for the Pi 3B+, 4 and 5 are based on the official documentation but have not been tested by me.

The Pi boots over the network and uses a virtual disk of a Proxmox VM as its root filesystem. From the Pi's point of view it is a normal block device (/dev/sda with ext4), from Proxmox's point of view it is just another VM disk. That gives you:

  • No SD card wear and no corrupted cards after power loss
  • Snapshots and Proxmox Backup Server (PBS) backups of the Pi like of any VM
  • Restoring a Pi = restoring a VM

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Step What happens Served by 1. DHCP Pi gets its IP and the address of the TFTP server (option 66) OPNsense (Dnsmasq) 2. TFTP Firmware loads config.txt, kernel and initramfs from a folder named after the Pi's serial number Netboot VM 3. iSCSI initramfs logs into the iSCSI target and mounts it as / Netboot VM 4. NFS The TFTP folder is mounted as /boot/firmware, so kernel updates land where the Pi boots from Netboot VM Why not NFS for the root filesystem?

NFS root is simpler to set up, but it is a file share, not a disk. Some software (Docker overlay storage, SQLite, file locking) behaves differently on NFS. iSCSI is a block device, the Pi formats it with ext4 itself and everything behaves like a local disk. A whole-disk restore via PBS also matches the "Pi = VM" idea better.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Pi 3B Pi 3B+ Pi 4 Pi 5 Network boot lives in Boot ROM (buggy) Boot ROM (fixed) EEPROM bootloader EEPROM bootloader Enable network boot OTP bit, permanent enabled from factory boot order in EEPROM, changeable any time same as Pi 4 SD card in operation tiny SD with only bootcode.bin (ROM bugs) none none none First TFTP request bootcode.bin (TFTP root) bootcode.bin (TFTP root) start4.elf in the serial-number folder files in the serial-number folder Kernel / initramfs (64-bit Pi OS) kernel8.img / initramfs8 kernel8.img / initramfs8 kernel8.img / initramfs8 kernel_2712.img / initramfs_2712 Ethernet 100 Mbit/s ~300 Mbit/s (behind USB 2.0) 1 Gbit/s 1 Gbit/s PoE HAT no yes yes yes

Tested target OS: Raspberry Pi OS Lite 64-bit. Netboot VM: Debian 13.

Why is the OTP bit on the Pi 3B permanent?

OTP means one-time programmable: tiny fuses inside the SoC. A bit can be burned from 0 to 1 once, there is no circuit to reset it.

The Pi 3 has no writable bootloader storage. Network boot is part of the boot ROM inside the chip, and the only persistent place the ROM can read a setting from before any OS runs is the OTP memory.

Raspberry Pi did not enable the new boot modes by default because they first wanted to check that they work as expected. Later, bugs showed up in the ROM, which were fixed in the 3B+. The 3B+ ships with the bit already set.

Setting it is harmless in practice: the SD card is still tried first. USB and network are only tried if no bootable SD card is present.

The Pi 4 and 5 have their own EEPROM bootloader, so the boot order is a normal setting there.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A DHCP server that can send option 66 (TFTP server) to the Pi. This guide uses OPNsense with Dnsmasq. If you are still on ISC DHCP, I recommend migrating since ISC is end-of-life: OPNsense: Migrate from ISC DHCP to Dnsmasq. ISC DHCP, Kea or any other DHCP server that can set option 66 works as well, only the menu paths differ.
  • The Netboot VM and the Pis must be in the same subnet. The Pi 3 boot ROM cannot reach a TFTP server through a router.
  • One SD card with Raspberry Pi OS Lite 64-bit for the initial setup of each Pi.

Values in angle brackets like <HOST> are placeholders. Every step that uses one has a box Values used in this step that tells you where to get it.

docs.title: 1.1 Create the Netboot VM
docs.text:
In the Proxmox GUI, on the node whose storage should hold the Pi disks:

Setting Value OS Debian 13 netinst, only SSH server + standard system utilities CPU / RAM 1 vCPU, 1 GB SCSI controller VirtIO SCSI single Disk scsi0 8 GB (system) Network same bridge/VLAN as the Pis Options Start at boot on, Start/Shutdown order 1

The disks for the Pis are added later, one per Pi.

Start order

The Pis cannot boot without this VM. Give it a low start order so it is up early after a node reboot.

docs.title: 1.2 Fixed IP for the VM (OPNsense)
docs.text:
Services → Dnsmasq DNS & DHCP → tab Hosts: add a fixed assignment for the VM (MAC from Proxmox → VM → Hardware → Network Device). Apply and restart the VM's network or reboot it.

From here on, this address is <VM-IP>. Example: 192.168.1.20.

docs.title: 1.3 Packages (VM)
docs.text:
apt install targetcli-fb dnsmasq nfs-kernel-server

Make the iSCSI configuration survive reboots: 

systemctl enable --now rtslib-fb-targetctl.service

docs.title: 1.4 TFTP server (VM)
docs.text:
Check the interface name with ip a (usually ens18).

/etc/dnsmasq.d/tftp.conf
# TFTP only, no DNS and no DHCP
port=0
interface=ens18
bind-interfaces
enable-tftp
tftp-root=/srv/tftp

Create the TFTP root before restarting, otherwise dnsmasq refuses to start (TFTP directory /srv/tftp inaccessible): 

mkdir -p /srv/tftp
systemctl restart dnsmasq
systemctl status dnsmasq --no-pager

docs.title: 1.5 TFTP server option (OPNsense)
docs.text:
Services → Dnsmasq DNS & DHCP

  1. Tab DHCP tags → + → Name: rpi → Save.

    Create the tag first

    The Tag fields in the other dialogs are dropdowns that only list existing tags. Typing a new name there only searches and shows No results matched.

  2. Tab DHCP options → + (bottom right of the table):

Field Value Interface Any Type Set Option tftp-server [66] Option6 None Tag rpi (select from the dropdown) Value <VM-IP> Force off

Apply. Only hosts with the rpi tag receive the TFTP server, other PXE clients in the network are not affected.

IP address, not a hostname

The Pi boot ROM has no DNS resolver. Option 66 must contain the IP address.

Different DHCP server

With ISC DHCP, Kea or another DHCP server, the goal is the same: the Pi's fixed assignment gets option 66 with the IP of the Netboot VM. Ideally only the Pis get it.

Why no ProxyDHCP?

Many guides run a second dnsmasq as ProxyDHCP next to the router. That exists for consumer routers that cannot send custom DHCP options. OPNsense can, so one DHCP server is enough. If a Pi hangs in DHCP or boot-loops, DHCP reply delay in Dnsmasq → General or a ProxyDHCP on the VM are possible workarounds.

docs.title: Part 2: Per Pi
docs.text:
Repeat this part for every Pi.

The SD card is only a workbench

You set up the Pi on an SD card first. Later, the whole system on that card is copied 1:1 to the iSCSI disk (root filesystem) and to the TFTP folder (kernel, initramfs, boot config). Everything installed and configured on the SD card, including the iSCSI client, ends up in the network-booted system. After the switch the card is no longer used.

Start with a fresh installation. An old card with random software and settings on it would be copied as well.

docs.title: 2.1 Install the Pi from SD card (Pi)
docs.text:
1. Raspberry Pi Imager: Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit), set hostname, user and SSH.

    The hostname is <HOST> from here on. Use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens only. Example: kitchen-pi.

  2. Boot the Pi from the SD card and update: 

    sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y && sudo reboot

docs.title: 2.2 Fixed IP and tag for the Pi (OPNsense)
docs.text:
Get the MAC address of the Pi (line link/ether, e.g. b8:27:eb:12:34:56): 

ip link show eth0

Services → Dnsmasq DNS & DHCP → tab Hosts: add a fixed assignment with this MAC and select rpi in Tag [set]. Apply.

This address is <PI-IP> from here on. Example: 192.168.1.50.

docs.title: 2.3 Enable network boot (Pi)
docs.text:
Pi 3BPi 3B+Pi 4 / Pi 5

Check the OTP bit: 

vcgencmd otp_dump | grep 17:

Output Meaning 17:3020000a already enabled 17:1020000a not enabled yet

Enable it (permanent, see Compatibility): 

echo "program_usb_boot_mode=1" | sudo tee -a /boot/firmware/config.txt
sudo reboot

Check again, it must show 17:3020000a. Then remove the line from /boot/firmware/config.txt so the card does not program other Pis by accident.

vcgencmd otp_dump | grep 17:

Must show 17:3020000a (factory default). If not, proceed as for the Pi 3B.

sudo raspi-config
  1. Advanced Options → Bootloader Version → Latest
  2. Advanced Options → Boot Order → Network Boot
  3. Exit and reboot.

Check: 

sudo rpi-eeprom-config
BOOT_ORDER must contain a 2, e.g. 0xf21 = SD card, then network, then retry.

docs.title: 2.4 Add a disk for the Pi (Proxmox)
docs.text:
Netboot VM → Hardware → Add → Hard Disk:

Setting Value Bus/Device SCSI, next free number (first Pi scsi1, second Pi scsi2, ...) Storage SSD storage, ideally LVM-thin or ZFS so snapshots and thin provisioning work Size 32 GB, see below Discard, SSD emulation on

On the VM, find the stable path of the new disk: 

ls -l /dev/disk/by-id/ | grep scsi

This path is <DISK> from here on. Example: /dev/disk/by-id/scsi-0QEMU_QEMU_HARDDISK_drive-scsi1.

Does the disk have to match the SD card size?

No. The system is copied file by file, not as a disk image. The VM disk only has to hold the data actually in use plus room to grow, the size of the SD card does not matter. A fresh Raspberry Pi OS Lite uses about 2 to 3 GB, check with df -h / on the Pi.

The disk can be enlarged later while the Pi is running:

  1. Proxmox → Netboot VM → Hardware → disk → Disk Action → Resize
  2. On the Pi, let iSCSI pick up the new size and grow the filesystem: 
    sudo iscsiadm -m session --rescan
sudo resize2fs /dev/sda

No partition needs to be resized because the disk has no partition table.

docs.title: 2.5 iSCSI target (VM)
docs.text:
Values used in this step

Placeholder Where to get it Example <HOST> hostname of the Pi: run hostname on the Pi kitchen-pi <DISK> path of the Pi's VM disk: run ls -l /dev/disk/by-id/ \| grep scsi on the VM /dev/disk/by-id/scsi-0QEMU_QEMU_HARDDISK_drive-scsi1 <IQN-PREFIX> iqn. + year-month + . + a domain you own, reversed. Same for every Pi iqn.2026-10.com.example

iSCSI identifies the target (VM side) and the initiator (Pi side) by an IQN. Both are built from the values above:

Name How to build it Example Target IQN <IQN-PREFIX>:netboot.<HOST> iqn.2026-10.com.example:netboot.kitchen-pi Initiator IQN <IQN-PREFIX>:<HOST> iqn.2026-10.com.example:kitchen-pi What is an IQN? 
iqn.2026-10.com.example:netboot.kitchen-pi
│   │       │           └─ free text
│   │       └─ a domain you own, reversed
│   └─ year and month you owned that domain
└─ fixed prefix

The date and domain only exist to make names globally unique. Neither the Pi nor the server checks them, they only compare the full string. Pick any domain you own and any date, and never change it afterwards.

Open targetcli: 

targetcli

Run inside targetcli:

TemplateExample targetcli
/backstores/block create name=<HOST> dev=<DISK>
/iscsi create <IQN-PREFIX>:netboot.<HOST>
/iscsi/<IQN-PREFIX>:netboot.<HOST>/tpg1/luns create /backstores/block/<HOST>
/iscsi/<IQN-PREFIX>:netboot.<HOST>/tpg1/acls create <IQN-PREFIX>:<HOST>
saveconfig
exit
targetcli
/backstores/block create name=kitchen-pi dev=/dev/disk/by-id/scsi-0QEMU_QEMU_HARDDISK_drive-scsi1
/iscsi create iqn.2026-10.com.example:netboot.kitchen-pi
/iscsi/iqn.2026-10.com.example:netboot.kitchen-pi/tpg1/luns create /backstores/block/kitchen-pi
/iscsi/iqn.2026-10.com.example:netboot.kitchen-pi/tpg1/acls create iqn.2026-10.com.example:kitchen-pi
saveconfig
exit
Command What it does backstores/block create registers the VM disk with the iSCSI service under an internal name iscsi create creates the target the Pi connects to luns create attaches the disk to the target acls create only an initiator with exactly this IQN may connect saveconfig saves everything Undo a step

Every create has a matching delete, e.g. /backstores/block delete <HOST>. Registering a backstore does not write anything to the disk itself. targetcli saves on exit by default, so a later delete is needed even after leaving the shell.

docs.title: 2.6 TFTP folder and NFS export (VM)
docs.text:
Values used in this step

Placeholder Where to get it Example <HOST> hostname of the Pi: run hostname on the Pi kitchen-pi <SERIAL> serial number of the Pi: run grep Serial /proc/cpuinfo on the Pi, take the last 8 characters, lowercase 00000000a1b2c3d4 → a1b2c3d4 <PI-IP> fixed IP of the Pi: OPNsense → Dnsmasq → Hosts, or hostname -I on the Pi 192.168.1.50

The Pi firmware requests its boot files from a TFTP folder named after its serial number. The real folder is named after the hostname, the serial number only becomes a symlink to it. Replacing a Pi later then means moving one symlink.

Why the serial number?

The boot firmware knows nothing about iSCSI or your configuration, it only knows its own serial number. Only the files loaded from that folder contain the iSCSI settings.

TemplateExample 
mkdir -p /srv/tftp/<HOST>
ln -s <HOST> /srv/tftp/<SERIAL>
ls -l /srv/tftp/

mkdir -p /srv/tftp/kitchen-pi
ln -s kitchen-pi /srv/tftp/a1b2c3d4
ls -l /srv/tftp/

ls must show the folder and the symlink pointing to it:

Example output
total 4
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root   10 Oct 25 16:39 a1b2c3d4 -> kitchen-pi
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Oct 25 16:41 kitchen-pi
Entry Meaning kitchen-pi (d at the start) real folder, the boot files go here later a1b2c3d4 -> kitchen-pi (l at the start) symlink named after the serial number, pointing to the folder. The number before the date is just the length of the target name

Export the hostname folder (never the symlink) to the Pi:

TemplateExample /etc/exports
/srv/tftp/<HOST>  <PI-IP>(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,no_root_squash)
/etc/exports
/srv/tftp/kitchen-pi  192.168.1.50(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,no_root_squash)

exportfs -ra

docs.title: 2.7 iSCSI client (Pi)
docs.text:
Values used in this step

Placeholder Where to get it Example <IQN-PREFIX> iqn. + year-month + . + a domain you own, reversed. Same for every Pi iqn.2026-10.com.example <HOST> hostname of the Pi: run hostname on the Pi kitchen-pi <VM-IP> IP of the Netboot VM: OPNsense → Dnsmasq → Hosts, or ip a on the VM 192.168.1.20 
sudo apt install open-iscsi nfs-common

nfs-common is needed to mount the TFTP folder as /boot/firmware via NFS.

The IQNs must be exactly the ones used for the iSCSI target on the VM:

TemplateExample /etc/iscsi/initiatorname.iscsi
InitiatorName=<IQN-PREFIX>:<HOST>
/etc/iscsi/initiatorname.iscsi
InitiatorName=iqn.2026-10.com.example:kitchen-pi
TemplateExample /etc/iscsi/iscsi.initramfs
ISCSI_INITIATOR=<IQN-PREFIX>:<HOST>
ISCSI_TARGET_NAME=<IQN-PREFIX>:netboot.<HOST>
ISCSI_TARGET_IP=<VM-IP>
ISCSI_TARGET_PORT=3260
/etc/iscsi/iscsi.initramfs
ISCSI_INITIATOR=iqn.2026-10.com.example:kitchen-pi
ISCSI_TARGET_NAME=iqn.2026-10.com.example:netboot.kitchen-pi
ISCSI_TARGET_IP=192.168.1.20
ISCSI_TARGET_PORT=3260

Change the existing lines in /etc/iscsi/iscsid.conf:

/etc/iscsi/iscsid.conf
node.session.timeo.replacement_timeout = -1  # queue I/O until the VM is back, never fail
node.conn[0].timeo.noop_out_interval = 0     # no keepalive pings, avoids recovery on short hiccups
node.conn[0].timeo.noop_out_timeout = 0      # same

The root session is created in the initramfs, so also set the timeout at boot:

/etc/tmpfiles.d/iscsi-timeout.conf
w /sys/class/iscsi_session/session*/recovery_tmo - - - - -1

Why wait forever?

The default replacement_timeout is 120 seconds. A negative value means: keep I/O queued until the session is logged in again, without any limit.

Timeout expires (default) -1 Pending writes fail, data is lost written as soon as the VM is back Filesystem ext4 switches to read-only stays writable Programs crash or hang with errors continue VM back again Pi stays broken, power-cycle needed Pi recovers by itself

While the VM is unreachable, programs that need the disk freeze, everything in RAM keeps running. The amount of unwritten data is limited by the kernel (vm.dirty_ratio): once the limit is reached, writing programs are paused, nothing is dropped. Data still in RAM is only lost if the Pi loses power during the outage.

There is no real downside: while the VM is gone, the Pi hangs either way. The only difference is that without a timeout it can recover by itself once the VM is back. With a timeout it stays broken and always needs a power-cycle.

Rebuild the initramfs and check: 

sudo update-initramfs -u
grep auto_initramfs /boot/firmware/config.txt
ls /boot/firmware/initramfs*
auto_initramfs=1 must be set (add it otherwise) and a fresh initramfs8 (Pi 3/4) or initramfs_2712 (Pi 5) must exist.

docs.title: 2.8 Connect and format the iSCSI disk (Pi)
docs.text:
Values used in this step

Placeholder Where to get it Example <VM-IP> IP of the Netboot VM: OPNsense → Dnsmasq → Hosts, or ip a on the VM 192.168.1.20 <IQN-PREFIX> iqn. + year-month + . + a domain you own, reversed. Same for every Pi iqn.2026-10.com.example <HOST> hostname of the Pi: run hostname on the Pi kitchen-pi TemplateExample 
sudo systemctl restart iscsid
sudo iscsiadm -m discovery -t st -p <VM-IP>
sudo iscsiadm -m node -T <IQN-PREFIX>:netboot.<HOST> -p <VM-IP> --login
lsblk

sudo systemctl restart iscsid
sudo iscsiadm -m discovery -t st -p 192.168.1.20
sudo iscsiadm -m node -T iqn.2026-10.com.example:netboot.kitchen-pi -p 192.168.1.20 --login
lsblk

The new 32 GB disk is /dev/sda, the SD card is mmcblk0. Format the whole disk without a partition table: 

sudo mkfs.ext4 -L piroot /dev/sda
sudo blkid /dev/sda

The value of UUID="..." is <UUID> from here on.

Example output
/dev/sda: LABEL="piroot" UUID="3f6c2b1e-8a4d-4c7e-9b21-5d0e7a9c4f12" BLOCK_SIZE="4096" TYPE="ext4"

docs.title: 2.9 Copy the system (Pi)
docs.text:
sudo mount /dev/sda /mnt
sudo rsync -aAXHx --info=progress2 / /mnt/
-x stays on the root filesystem. /boot/firmware, /proc, /sys, /dev and /run are created as empty folders only.

docs.title: 2.10 fstab on the iSCSI disk (Pi)
docs.text:
Values used in this step

Placeholder Where to get it Example <UUID> UUID of the iSCSI disk: run sudo blkid /dev/sda on the Pi, value of UUID="..." 3f6c2b1e-8a4d-4c7e-9b21-5d0e7a9c4f12 <VM-IP> IP of the Netboot VM: OPNsense → Dnsmasq → Hosts, or ip a on the VM 192.168.1.20 <HOST> hostname of the Pi: run hostname on the Pi kitchen-pi

Replace the whole file:

TemplateExample /mnt/etc/fstab
proc  /proc  proc  defaults  0 0
UUID=<UUID>  /  ext4  defaults,noatime,_netdev  0 1
<VM-IP>:/srv/tftp/<HOST>  /boot/firmware  nfs  defaults,_netdev  0 0
/mnt/etc/fstab
proc  /proc  proc  defaults  0 0
UUID=3f6c2b1e-8a4d-4c7e-9b21-5d0e7a9c4f12  /  ext4  defaults,noatime,_netdev  0 1
192.168.1.20:/srv/tftp/kitchen-pi  /boot/firmware  nfs  defaults,_netdev  0 0

docs.title: 2.11 Boot files to the TFTP folder (Pi)
docs.text:
Values used in this step

Placeholder Where to get it Example <VM-IP> IP of the Netboot VM: OPNsense → Dnsmasq → Hosts, or ip a on the VM 192.168.1.20 <HOST> hostname of the Pi: run hostname on the Pi kitchen-pi <UUID> UUID of the iSCSI disk: run sudo blkid /dev/sda on the Pi, value of UUID="..." 3f6c2b1e-8a4d-4c7e-9b21-5d0e7a9c4f12 TemplateExample 
sudo mkdir -p /mnt2
sudo mount -t nfs <VM-IP>:/srv/tftp/<HOST> /mnt2
sudo rsync -rlt /boot/firmware/ /mnt2/

sudo mkdir -p /mnt2
sudo mount -t nfs 192.168.1.20:/srv/tftp/kitchen-pi /mnt2
sudo rsync -rlt /boot/firmware/ /mnt2/

In cmdline.txt, change only the root device and add ip=dhcp. Everything else stays as it is (WiFi region, cloud-init settings from the Raspberry Pi Imager, etc.):

Before After root=PARTUUID=... (SD card) ip=dhcp root=UUID=<UUID> (iSCSI disk, network up in the initramfs) TemplateExample 
sudo sed -i 's|root=PARTUUID=[^ ]*|ip=dhcp root=UUID=<UUID>|' /mnt2/cmdline.txt
cat /mnt2/cmdline.txt

sudo sed -i 's|root=PARTUUID=[^ ]*|ip=dhcp root=UUID=3f6c2b1e-8a4d-4c7e-9b21-5d0e7a9c4f12|' /mnt2/cmdline.txt
cat /mnt2/cmdline.txt

The file must still be one single line:

Example result
console=serial0,115200 console=tty1 ip=dhcp root=UUID=3f6c2b1e-8a4d-4c7e-9b21-5d0e7a9c4f12 rootfstype=ext4 fsck.repair=yes rootwait cfg80211.ieee80211_regdom=DE ds=nocloud;i=rpi-imager-1234567890
What is ds=nocloud;i=...?

Since Raspberry Pi OS Trixie, the Raspberry Pi Imager applies its settings (user, SSH, WiFi, ...) via cloud-init on the first boot. This parameter tells cloud-init where its data is and which instance it belongs to. Keep it unchanged: cloud-init then knows the setup already ran and does not apply it again.

docs.title: 2.12 bootcode.bin in the TFTP root (VM, Pi 3B / 3B+ only, once)
docs.text:
Values used in this step

Placeholder Where to get it Example <HOST> hostname of the Pi: run hostname on the Pi kitchen-pi

The Pi 3 needs bootcode.bin before anything else. Who reads it from where:

Model Reads bootcode.bin from Copy in the TFTP root needed? Pi 3B+ TFTP root (/srv/tftp/bootcode.bin) yes Pi 3B with tiny SD card the tiny SD card (step 2.13) no, but it is the easiest source for creating that card Pi 4 / 5 not used no

Copy it from the Pi's boot files into the TFTP root:

TemplateExample 
cp /srv/tftp/<HOST>/bootcode.bin /srv/tftp/

cp /srv/tftp/kitchen-pi/bootcode.bin /srv/tftp/

If cp reports No such file or directory, your Raspberry Pi OS image does not ship the file. Get it from the official Raspberry Pi firmware repository instead: 

wget -O /srv/tftp/bootcode.bin https://github.com/raspberrypi/firmware/raw/master/boot/bootcode.bin

bootcode.bin is not specific to a Pi: it contains no serial number, hostname or configuration and is identical for every Pi 3. One copy in the TFTP root serves all Pi 3 on this VM, so this step is only needed once. Keep it there, it is only about 50 KB.

docs.title: 2.13 Switch over (Pi)
docs.text:
Unmount everything and shut down the Pi: 

sudo umount /mnt2 /mnt
sudo iscsiadm -m node -u
sudo poweroff

Keep the SD card with the full system as a fallback.

Pi 3BPi 3B+ / 4 / 5

The Pi 3B needs a tiny SD card that contains nothing but bootcode.bin. Its boot ROM has network boot bugs, the newer bootcode.bin from the card works around them. The card is only read at boot, never written, so wear is not an issue. Any size works. Since bootcode.bin is the same for every Pi 3, the card is not tied to this Pi either: it works in any Pi 3B, and you can prepare several identical cards in advance.

Do this on a Linux PC.

Values used in this step

Placeholder Where to get it Example <VM-IP> IP of the Netboot VM: OPNsense → Dnsmasq → Hosts, or ip a on the VM 192.168.1.20 <SD-DEVICE> the SD card: insert it and run lsblk, it is the new disk with the matching size /dev/sdc

  1. Get bootcode.bin from the VM:

    TemplateExample 
    scp root@<VM-IP>:/srv/tftp/bootcode.bin .

    scp root@192.168.1.20:/srv/tftp/bootcode.bin .

  2. Prepare the card: one FAT32 partition, nothing else.

    GUI: KDE Partition Manager or GNOME Disks → select the SD card → new partition table MS-DOS (MBR) → one partition over the whole card, filesystem FAT32 → apply. Then copy bootcode.bin to the card in the file manager.

    CLI:

    Check <SD-DEVICE> twice

    These commands erase the whole device. A wrong device name wipes another disk.

    TemplateExample 
    lsblk
sudo umount <SD-DEVICE>*
sudo wipefs -a <SD-DEVICE>
sudo parted -s <SD-DEVICE> mklabel msdos mkpart primary fat32 1MiB 100%
sudo mkfs.vfat -F 32 <SD-DEVICE>1
sudo mount <SD-DEVICE>1 /mnt
sudo cp bootcode.bin /mnt/
ls /mnt
sudo umount /mnt

    lsblk
sudo umount /dev/sdc*
sudo wipefs -a /dev/sdc
sudo parted -s /dev/sdc mklabel msdos mkpart primary fat32 1MiB 100%
sudo mkfs.vfat -F 32 /dev/sdc1
sudo mount /dev/sdc1 /mnt
sudo cp bootcode.bin /mnt/
ls /mnt
sudo umount /mnt

    ls /mnt must show only bootcode.bin.

  3. Insert the tiny SD card into the Pi. It stays there permanently.

Remove the SD card. Nothing else is needed.

Power on the Pi.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Where Command Expected VM journalctl -u dnsmasq -f while the Pi boots Pi 3: sent .../bootcode.bin, then files from the serial-number folder. Pi 4/5: files from the serial-number folder directly Pi 4/5 HDMI screen during boot diagnostics screen shows IP, TFTP server and serial number Pi sudo iscsiadm -m session one session to the target Pi findmnt / and findmnt /boot/firmware /dev/sda and NFS Pi cat /sys/class/iscsi_session/session1/recovery_tmo -1

Enable TRIM so deleted space is returned to the thin-provisioned VM disk: 

sudo systemctl enable --now fstrim.timer

docs.title: Swap only in RAM (Pi)
docs.text:
Since Raspberry Pi OS Trixie, swap is managed by rpi-swap. The default Mechanism=auto currently resolves to zram+file: a compressed swap area in RAM (zram), plus a file /var/swap that rarely used pages are written to later. With network boot, that file lives on the iSCSI disk, so every write goes over the network and a VM outage also freezes swapped-out programs.

I recommend keeping zram but dropping the file:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d
printf '[Main]\nMechanism=zram\n' | sudo tee /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/90-zram-only.conf
sudo reboot
All values for Mechanism Value Behaviour auto (default) currently zram+file, may change in future releases zram compressed swap in RAM only, all [File] options are ignored zram+file zram plus /var/swap as writeback storage for idle pages swapfile classic swap file on the root filesystem none no swap, an existing swap file is removed

After the reboot: 

swapon --show
Must show /dev/zram0 only. A leftover /var/swap can be deleted with sudo rm /var/swap.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause / fix No TFTP requests in the dnsmasq log Pi host lacks the rpi tag, option 66 missing, or Pi and VM in different subnets file .../<SERIAL>/... not found symlink missing or wrong. Check ls -l /srv/tftp/, serial in lowercase? Pi 3B boots unreliably without the tiny SD card expected, boot ROM bug. Use the SD card with bootcode.bin Pi hangs in DHCP or boot-loops boot ROM timing bug. Try DHCP reply delay in Dnsmasq → General Pi 4/5 does not try network boot BOOT_ORDER without 2, or outdated bootloader (step 2.3) Waiting for root device initramfs without iSCSI (step 2.7 done before 2.9?), or ACL IQN does not match the Pi IQN Pi loses the connection shortly after boot NetworkManager reconfigures eth0. Mark eth0 as unmanaged in NetworkManager Boot fails after a kernel update /boot/firmware was not mounted via NFS during the update

docs.title: Operation
docs.text: Situation What to do Short reboot of the Proxmox node nothing, the Pi freezes and continues afterwards Longer maintenance shut down the Pis first Pi hangs after an outage power-cycle it. Pi 3B+/4/5 with a PoE HAT via the switch port, Pi 3B via a smart plug Backup the PBS backup of the Netboot VM contains all Pi disks (crash-consistent) Restore restoring the Netboot VM restores all Pis. For a single Pi: restore to a new VMID and reassign only its disk Performance the Pi 3B with 100 Mbit/s is not suited for databases or heavy I/O

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
The system does not live on the Pi, so almost everything can be repaired from the Netboot VM without touching the Pi hardware.

Problem Where to fix it Pi does not boot after a change to cmdline.txt or config.txt Fix the boot files Broken fstab, network config or other system file Fix files on the root disk Broken package or system update, commands needed Run commands in the Pi system Everything broken Roll back You want to see what happens during boot See the boot process

docs.title: Fix the boot files
docs.text:
Values used in this step

Placeholder Where to get it Example <HOST> hostname of the Pi, also the folder name in /srv/tftp/ on the VM: ls -l /srv/tftp/ kitchen-pi

The boot files are plain files on the VM. Edit them directly, then power-cycle the Pi.

TemplateExample 
nano /srv/tftp/<HOST>/cmdline.txt
nano /srv/tftp/<HOST>/config.txt

nano /srv/tftp/kitchen-pi/cmdline.txt
nano /srv/tftp/kitchen-pi/config.txt

docs.title: Fix files on the root disk
docs.text:
Values used in this step

Placeholder Where to get it Example <DISK> path of the Pi's VM disk: run ls -l /dev/disk/by-id/ \| grep scsi on the VM /dev/disk/by-id/scsi-0QEMU_QEMU_HARDDISK_drive-scsi1

Only while the Pi is off

Never mount the disk on the VM while the Pi is using it. Two systems writing to the same ext4 filesystem destroy it.

  1. Shut down the Pi, or cut its power if it hangs.

  2. On the VM, check that no iSCSI session is active anymore: 

    targetcli sessions
    It must report (no open sessions). After cutting the power this can take up to about a minute.

  3. Release the disk from the iSCSI service. As long as the target is active, it holds the disk exclusively and mount fails with Can't open blockdev: 

    targetcli saveconfig
targetctl clear

    Affects all Pis

    This stops the iSCSI target for every Pi on this VM. Running Pis freeze and continue once the target is restored in step 5.

  4. Mount the disk, fix the file, unmount. Use the by-id path, /dev/disk/by-uuid/... does not exist on the VM because the Pi formatted the disk over iSCSI and the VM never noticed:

TemplateExample 
mount <DISK> /mnt
nano /mnt/etc/fstab
umount /mnt

mount /dev/disk/by-id/scsi-0QEMU_QEMU_HARDDISK_drive-scsi1 /mnt
nano /mnt/etc/fstab
umount /mnt

  1. Restore the iSCSI target and check that it is back: 

    targetctl restore
targetcli ls
    targetcli ls must show the backstore, the target with its ACL and the LUN again. Without this step no Pi can boot.

  2. Power on the Pi.

docs.title: Run commands in the Pi system
docs.text:
Values used in this step

Placeholder Where to get it Example <DISK> path of the Pi's VM disk: run ls -l /dev/disk/by-id/ \| grep scsi on the VM /dev/disk/by-id/scsi-0QEMU_QEMU_HARDDISK_drive-scsi1 <HOST> hostname of the Pi, also the folder name in /srv/tftp/ on the VM kitchen-pi

When files alone are not enough (e.g. a broken package), you can run the Pi's own programs on the VM. The VM is x86, the Pi system is ARM, so qemu-user-static emulates the ARM binaries. Slow, but apt, dpkg and update-initramfs work.

Same rules as above: the Pi must be off (targetcli sessions shows (no open sessions)).

Release the disk from the iSCSI service (affects all Pis on this VM): 

targetcli saveconfig
targetctl clear

Once, on the VM: 

apt install qemu-user-static

Mount the disk, the boot files and the system folders, then switch into the Pi system:

TemplateExample 
mount <DISK> /mnt
mount --bind /srv/tftp/<HOST> /mnt/boot/firmware
for d in proc sys dev dev/pts; do mount --bind /$d /mnt/$d; done
chroot /mnt /bin/bash

mount /dev/disk/by-id/scsi-0QEMU_QEMU_HARDDISK_drive-scsi1 /mnt
mount --bind /srv/tftp/kitchen-pi /mnt/boot/firmware
for d in proc sys dev dev/pts; do mount --bind /$d /mnt/$d; done
chroot /mnt /bin/bash

Check that you are inside the Pi system, it must show aarch64: 

uname -m

Repair, e.g. dpkg --configure -a or apt install --reinstall <package>. Then leave, unmount everything and restore the iSCSI target: 

exit
umount -R /mnt
targetctl restore
targetcli ls

docs.title: Roll back
docs.text:
Method When Proxmox snapshot of the Netboot VM quick undo after a risky change. Take the snapshot before the change PBS restore older state. Restoring the whole VM affects all Pis. For a single Pi: restore to a new VMID and move only its disk to the Netboot VM

Shut down the affected Pis before rolling back. The boot files in /srv/tftp/ are on the VM's system disk and are rolled back with the VM, not with the Pi disk.

docs.title: See the boot process
docs.text:
Method Extra hardware What you see journalctl -u dnsmasq -f on the VM no whether the Pi requests its boot files and which ones Serial console USB-UART adapter on the Pi's GPIO pins, connected to another computer nearby the complete boot including initramfs, also when the network fails. console=serial0,115200 is already in cmdline.txt Network KVM (e.g. PiKVM, NanoKVM, JetKVM) on HDMI yes, permanently attached screen and keyboard in the browser Kernel log over the network (netconsole, untested)

The kernel can send its messages via UDP to another host. On the Pi, netconsole is a kernel module, so it has to be in the initramfs and configured with the module syntax.

On the Pi: 

echo netconsole | sudo tee -a /etc/initramfs-tools/modules
sudo update-initramfs -u

Append to cmdline.txt (same single line), with the IP of the VM (<VM-IP>, e.g. 192.168.1.20):

TemplateExample 
netconsole.netconsole=@/eth0,6666@<VM-IP>/

netconsole.netconsole=@/eth0,6666@192.168.1.20/

Listen on the VM: 

apt install netcat-openbsd
nc -klu 6666

Messages start once the network driver is up, so very early boot errors are not covered. Not tested with this setup yet.

docs.title: Replace a Pi
docs.text:
A new Pi has a new serial number and a new MAC address. The iSCSI disk, target and IQN stay the same, so the new Pi boots exactly the old system.

Item Changes? iSCSI disk, target, IQN no /etc/exports, fstab no (they point to the hostname folder) symlink <SERIAL> yes MAC in OPNsense yes
  1. Shut down and disconnect the old Pi.
  2. Prepare the new Pi:
Model Preparation Pi 3B boot once from a normal SD card, set the OTP bit (step 2.3), note the serial. Then insert the tiny SD card with bootcode.bin Pi 3B+ boot once from a normal SD card and note the serial Pi 4 / 5 boot once from a normal SD card, enable network boot (step 2.3), note the serial
  1. Move the symlink on the VM. Old and new serial: run grep Serial /proc/cpuinfo on each Pi (booted from SD), last 8 characters, lowercase. <HOST> stays the same.
TemplateExample 
rm /srv/tftp/<OLD-SERIAL>
ln -s <HOST> /srv/tftp/<NEW-SERIAL>

rm /srv/tftp/a1b2c3d4
ln -s kitchen-pi /srv/tftp/e5f6a7b8
  1. OPNsense → Dnsmasq → Hosts → entry of the Pi → new MAC → Apply. IP and tag stay.
  2. Power on the new Pi.

Changing the model

64-bit Raspberry Pi OS ships the firmware and kernels for all models, so the same disk usually boots on a Pi 3, 4 or 5. Run sudo update-initramfs -u -k all on the old Pi first, so the iSCSI initramfs exists for every kernel. A Pi 3 additionally needs bootcode.bin in the TFTP root (step 2.12).

Alternative for Pi 4 / 5 only

The EEPROM setting TFTP_PREFIX can make the firmware use a fixed string or the MAC address instead of the serial number as folder name. The symlink works the same way for every model, so this guide sticks with it.

docs.title: OPNsense: Migrate from ISC DHCP to Dnsmasq
OPNsense: Migrate from ISC DHCP to Dnsmasq
docs.text:
AI-generated guide

This guide and the lease conversion script were written by an AI. I did not write the text myself. I did, however, carry out the procedure exactly as described on my production OPNsense 26.7 with five VLANs, 21 static mappings and 76 active leases, and verified the result afterwards.

ISC DHCP has been end-of-life since 2022. OPNsense still ships it (marked as [legacy] in the menu), but new installations use Dnsmasq since 25.7 and ISC will eventually move out of the core.

This guide migrates an existing multi-VLAN setup from ISC DHCPv4 to Dnsmasq. It also covers something most guides skip: taking over the active leases, so Dnsmasq knows which addresses are in use from the first second instead of waiting until every client has renewed.

docs.title: Why Dnsmasq and not Kea
docs.text:
OPNsense offers both. For a home or small office network Dnsmasq is probably the better fit:

Dnsmasq Kea OPNsense default for new installs yes (since 25.7) no PXE / network boot options in the GUI yes no Registers dynamic client names in DNS yes static reservations only Dynamic IPv6 prefix tracking yes no High availability / failover no yes

Unless you need DHCP failover, pick Dnsmasq.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Rollback is always possible

Disable Dnsmasq, re-enable ISC on all interfaces. Clients keep their leases until they expire, so there is no hard outage at any point of this migration.

  • Backup: System → Configuration → Backups → Download configuration
  • Work from a device with a static IP or a fixed DHCP assignment so you can always reach the GUI
  • If you have IPv6 via SLAAC (Router Advertisements) and ISC DHCPv6 is disabled, IPv6 is not affected at all. Do not create IPv6 ranges in Dnsmasq.

docs.title: 1. Collect the ISC values
docs.text:
For every interface under Services → ISC DHCPv4 → [Interface], note:

ISC field Goes to Range from / to Dnsmasq → DHCP ranges Additional Pools one extra range each DNS servers (if filled) Dnsmasq → DHCP options, option 6 DNS servers (empty) means "system DNS", you have to set option 6 explicitly in Dnsmasq Gateway (empty) nothing, Dnsmasq defaults to the interface IP as well Default lease time Dnsmasq range → Lease time (empty = 86400 s) NTP servers option 42 Static mappings count them for the import check

Interfaces without ISC config

The Dnsmasq interface dropdown lists every interface. Only select the ones that actually had an ISC instance.

docs.title: 2. Export the static mappings
docs.text:
Services → ISC DHCPv4 → [Interface] → download icon below the static mappings table.

The export is one CSV per interface with the columns ip_address,hw_address,hostname,description. Merge them into one file and check for:

  • Duplicate hostnames: Dnsmasq registers names in DNS, give each host a unique name
  • Same MAC in several subnets (e.g. a test VM): fine, Dnsmasq picks the entry matching the subnet, and the GUI import accepts it

docs.title: 3. Dnsmasq → General
docs.text:
Services → Dnsmasq DNS & DHCP → General, enable advanced mode.

Setting Value Enable leave off until step 7. Dnsmasq cannot bind port 67 while ISC is running Interface every interface that had ISC enabled DNS → Listen port 0 if another resolver (Pi-hole, Unbound, AdGuard) stays in charge. This disables the Dnsmasq DNS part completely DHCP → DHCP FQDN on DHCP → DHCP default domain shows your system domain, cannot be empty DHCP → DHCP local domain on DHCP → DHCP authoritative on (Dnsmasq is the only DHCP server) DHCP → DHCP register firewall rules on DHCP → Router advertisements off if radvd handles IPv6 ISC / KEA DHCP (legacy) all off

Apply.

Authoritative and network boot

Authoritative means Dnsmasq answers requests for unknown leases instead of ignoring them. A TFTP server or a ProxyDHCP for PXE boot is not a second DHCP server, so this setting is correct even with network boot in place.

docs.title: 4. DHCP ranges
docs.text:
Tab DHCP ranges, one entry per interface. Leave Subnet mask on automatic, Constructor on None, Tag and Domain empty.

Field Value Interface the interface Start / End address the ISC range Lease time empty for the default, or your ISC value Description e.g. LAN IPv4

Example for a typical setup:

Interface Start End Lease time LAN 192.168.1.150 192.168.1.254 86400 IoT 192.168.5.50 192.168.5.254 31536000 Guest 192.168.10.50 192.168.10.254 86400 Long lease times are no longer needed for stable IoT addresses

Under ISC a one-year lease is a common trick to keep IoT devices on the same address without creating a static mapping for every single one. Dnsmasq derives the offered address from a hash of the MAC address, so a device gets its old address again even after the lease expired and was forgotten. You can keep the long lease, but it now only controls how long a replaced device stays visible in the lease list.

docs.title: 5. Import the static mappings
docs.text:
Tab Hosts → upload icon (bottom right) → your merged CSV. Compare the row count, open two or three entries and check MAC, IP and hostname. Apply.

Reservations outside the dynamic range keep working as long as a range exists in the same subnet. You do not have to renumber anything.

docs.title: 6. DHCP options
docs.text: Tab DHCP options, section Options. Type Set, Tag empty, Force off.

docs.title: DNS (option 6)
docs.text:
ISC used the system DNS servers when the field was empty. Dnsmasq does not do this reliably, so set it explicitly. If some networks use different resolvers (e.g. a dedicated Pi-hole for IoT), create one entry per interface:

Interface Option Value LAN dns-server [6] 192.168.1.3,192.168.1.4 Guest dns-server [6] 192.168.1.3,192.168.1.4 IoT dns-server [6] 192.168.1.6,192.168.1.7

docs.title: NTP (option 42)
docs.text:
One entry covers all networks:

Interface Option Value (empty = all) ntp-server [42] 0.0.0.0

0.0.0.0 means 'this interface'

Dnsmasq replaces 0.0.0.0 with the address of the interface the request came in on. Works for any option that takes an IP address. Under ISC you had to enter the interface IP on every single interface.

Apply.

docs.title: 7. Switch over and take over the active leases
docs.text:
Dnsmasq starts with an empty lease table. Without a takeover it would not know which addresses ISC has handed out until every client renews. With day-long leases that is fine, with year-long IoT leases it means months of blind spots in which Dnsmasq might offer an address that is actually in use (it pings first, but sleeping devices do not answer).

The script below converts the active ISC leases into the Dnsmasq lease file format. Nothing runs on the firewall itself, you only copy two files.

# Where Action 1 GUI Services → ISC DHCPv4 → [each interface]: untick Enable → Save 2 PC scp root@<opnsense>:/var/dhcpd/var/db/dhcpd.leases ./dhcpd.leases 3 PC python3 isc2dnsmasq_leases.py --isc ./dhcpd.leases --out ./dnsmasq.leases --force 4 PC scp ./dnsmasq.leases root@<opnsense>:/var/db/dnsmasq.leases 5 GUI Services → Dnsmasq DNS & DHCP → General → Enable → Save → Apply 6 GUI Tab Leases: the imported leases show up immediately

Do steps 1 to 5 in one go. Clients keep working on their existing leases in the meantime.

--force only skips the check for running dnsmasq/dhcpd processes, which is meant for running the script on the firewall itself. On your PC it would otherwise trip over a local dnsmasq from libvirt or NetworkManager.

Lease file path

OPNsense does not set dhcp-leasefile, so Dnsmasq uses the FreeBSD default /var/db/dnsmasq.leases. ISC runs chrooted, its lease file is /var/dhcpd/var/db/dhcpd.leases.

isc2dnsmasq_leases.py

What it does: keeps the last block per IP (ISC appends new states), takes only binding state active, skips leases expiring within 10 minutes, turns ends never into expiry 0 (infinite), strips domain parts from hostnames and writes * as client ID. Dnsmasq matches such leases by MAC and fills in the client ID on the first renewal. An existing output file is backed up first.

isc2dnsmasq_leases.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Convert active ISC dhcpd leases into a dnsmasq lease file.

dnsmasq lease file format (one line per lease):
    <expiry-epoch> <mac> <ip> <hostname|*> <client-id|*>
An expiry of 0 means "never expires".

Usage:
    python3 isc2dnsmasq_leases.py --isc dhcpd.leases --out dnsmasq.leases --dry-run
    python3 isc2dnsmasq_leases.py --isc dhcpd.leases --out dnsmasq.leases --force
"""

import argparse
import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone

DEFAULT_ISC = "/var/dhcpd/var/db/dhcpd.leases"
DEFAULT_OUT = "/var/db/dnsmasq.leases"

HOSTNAME_RE = re.compile(r"[^A-Za-z0-9-]")


def parse_isc_leases(path):
    """Return {ip: lease_dict} keeping the LAST block per IP (ISC appends)."""
    with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as fh:
        text = fh.read()

    leases = {}
    for match in re.finditer(r"lease\s+(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)\s*\{(.*?)\n\}", text, re.S):
        ip, body = match.group(1), match.group(2)
        lease = {"ip": ip, "ends": None, "never": False, "state": None,
                 "mac": None, "hostname": None}

        m = re.search(r"^\s*ends\s+(never|\d\s+[\d/]+\s+[\d:]+);", body, re.M)
        if m:
            if m.group(1) == "never":
                lease["never"] = True
            else:
                _, date_s, time_s = m.group(1).split()
                dt = datetime.strptime(f"{date_s} {time_s}", "%Y/%m/%d %H:%M:%S")
                lease["ends"] = int(dt.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).timestamp())

        m = re.search(r"^\s*binding state\s+(\w+);", body, re.M)
        if m:
            lease["state"] = m.group(1)

        m = re.search(r"^\s*hardware ethernet\s+([0-9a-fA-F:]+);", body, re.M)
        if m:
            lease["mac"] = m.group(1).lower()

        m = re.search(r'^\s*client-hostname\s+"([^"]*)";', body, re.M)
        if m:
            lease["hostname"] = m.group(1)

        leases[ip] = lease
    return leases


def sanitize_hostname(name):
    if not name:
        return "*"
    name = name.split(".")[0]
    name = HOSTNAME_RE.sub("-", name).strip("-")
    return name or "*"


def process_running(name):
    try:
        subprocess.run(["pgrep", "-x", name], check=True,
                       stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
        return True
    except subprocess.CalledProcessError:
        return False


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__,
                                 formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument("--isc", default=DEFAULT_ISC, help="ISC dhcpd.leases path")
    ap.add_argument("--out", default=DEFAULT_OUT, help="dnsmasq lease file path")
    ap.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true", help="print result, write nothing")
    ap.add_argument("--min-remaining", type=int, default=600,
                    help="skip leases expiring within N seconds (default 600)")
    ap.add_argument("--force", action="store_true",
                    help="write even if dnsmasq or dhcpd is running")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    if not os.path.exists(args.isc):
        sys.exit(f"ERROR: ISC lease file not found: {args.isc}")

    now = int(time.time())
    all_leases = parse_isc_leases(args.isc)

    out_lines = []
    skipped = {"inactive": 0, "expired": 0, "no_mac": 0}
    for ip in sorted(all_leases, key=lambda s: tuple(int(o) for o in s.split("."))):
        l = all_leases[ip]
        if l["state"] != "active":
            skipped["inactive"] += 1
            continue
        if not l["mac"]:
            skipped["no_mac"] += 1
            continue
        if l["never"]:
            expiry = 0
        else:
            if l["ends"] is None or l["ends"] - now < args.min_remaining:
                skipped["expired"] += 1
                continue
            expiry = l["ends"]
        out_lines.append(f"{expiry} {l['mac']} {ip} {sanitize_hostname(l['hostname'])} *")

    print(f"Parsed {len(all_leases)} lease blocks from {args.isc}")
    print(f"Active leases to import: {len(out_lines)}")
    print(f"Skipped: {skipped['inactive']} inactive, {skipped['expired']} expired/short, "
          f"{skipped['no_mac']} without MAC")
    print("-" * 60)
    for line in out_lines:
        print(line)
    print("-" * 60)

    if args.dry_run:
        print("Dry run, nothing written.")
        return

    if not args.force:
        if process_running("dnsmasq"):
            sys.exit("ERROR: dnsmasq is running. Disable it first or use --force.")
        if process_running("dhcpd"):
            sys.exit("ERROR: ISC dhcpd is still running, leases may still change. "
                     "Disable ISC DHCPv4 on all interfaces first or use --force.")

    if os.path.exists(args.out):
        backup = f"{args.out}.bak-{time.strftime('%Y%m%d-%H%M%S')}"
        os.replace(args.out, backup)
        print(f"Existing lease file moved to {backup}")

    tmp = args.out + ".tmp"
    with open(tmp, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        fh.write("\n".join(out_lines) + ("\n" if out_lines else ""))
    os.chmod(tmp, 0o644)
    os.replace(tmp, args.out)
    print(f"Wrote {len(out_lines)} leases to {args.out}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: 8. Verify
docs.text:
1. Renew a lease on a client: 
    nmcli con down "<connection>" && nmcli con up "<connection>"
  2. Check address, gateway and DNS: 
    nmcli dev show | grep -E 'IP4.ADDRESS|IP4.GATEWAY|IP4.DNS'
  3. A client with a fixed assignment shows up in the Leases tab with Lease Type static.
  4. Over the next days, confirm that IoT devices keep their addresses after a reboot.

Side effect you will probably notice: reconnects are a lot faster. ISC syncs its lease file on every transaction and hooks into other services, Dnsmasq answers known clients straight from memory.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
1. Dnsmasq → General → Enable off → Apply
  2. ISC DHCPv4 → Enable on every interface → Save
  3. Read Services → Dnsmasq DNS & DHCP → Log File, fix the cause, try again from step 7

docs.title: Afterwards
docs.text:
• ISC stays installed: as of 26.7 it is still part of the OPNsense core and cannot be uninstalled. Disabled on all interfaces, dhcpd simply does not run. When a future release moves it to a plugin, do not install that plugin.
  • Local hostname resolution: with the Dnsmasq DNS part disabled, your resolver does not know the DHCP client names. If you want that, enable Dnsmasq DNS on a side port (e.g. 53053, not 5353 which is mDNS) and forward your local domain from Pi-hole/Unbound to 127.0.0.1:53053.
  • Network boot: Dnsmasq has the PXE options in the GUI (DHCP boot, DHCP tags). A TFTP server next to it is enough, no second DHCP server needed.

docs.title: Specific (Wi-Fi) Network works for few seconds, breaks, then works again for few seconds
Specific (Wi-Fi) Network works for few seconds, breaks, then works again for few seconds
Story
docs.text:
So I had really weird network problems on one specific Wi-Fi network on my laptop running Kubuntu.

The problem was that the network worked a few seconds after connecting, then stopped working for a few seconds and then come back for a few seconds, over and over again. Sometimes it would not recover though. Even using ping, the responses were interrupted, so a DNS or firewall problems seemed unlikely. The connection status was still connected. Because the network requires PEAP authentication, I thought that this would be the problem (especially because it worked on all other devices I had).

But after trying all kinds of things, thinking it the network would block something or an authentication issue, the problem was rather simple.

Turns out, Docker, which was running on my laptop, was the problem because it was using the same network range (127.x.x.x).

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
To verify that Docker was actually causing this issue, I have stopped it and deleted the network (will be recreated automatically when starting Docker again): 

sudo systemctl stop docker
sudo ip link delete docker0

Directly after executing these commands, the network instantly worked flawlessly. To keep using Docker while on this network, we need to change the Docker subnet.

Create/Modify this file and add this option:

/etc/docker/daemon.json
{
  "bip": "192.168.100.1/24"
}

Then restart Docker: 

sudo systemctl restart docker

docs.title: iperf3: Network speed tests
docs.text: iperf 3 is a useful tool that allows you to easily do (local) network speed tests between two computers.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
iperf3 -s
After executing this command, the server is started and no longer needs to be touched. All the test related options are used from the client side.

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
To start a basic upload (client -> server) speed test, type this command: 

iperf3 -c x.x.x.x
Replace x.x.x.x with the IP address of the server.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
You can add options to the client command to e.g. reverse the speed test (upload/download) or do a bidirectional speed test (upload and download at the same time).

Here is a short list of the probably most used options:

Option Description -R Run in reverse mode (server sends, client receives) --bidir Run in bidirectional mode -t 30 Time in seconds (e.g. 30s) to transmit for (default 10 secs)

To get the full list of options + descriptions, type: 

iperf3 --help

docs.title: Run as service
docs.text:
To always let the server run without opening a terminal, you can create an iperf3 service that automatically gets started on boot.

Create this file:

/etc/systemd/system/iperf3.service
[Unit]
Description=iperf3 server
After=syslog.target network.target auditd.service

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/iperf3 -s

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Reload systemctl (this is needed after creating/modifying systemd service files): 

systemctl daemon-reload

Start the iperf3 server: 

systemctl start iperf3

Enable it so that it automatically start back up on reboot: 

systemctl enable iperf3
